interest: Japan estimated 30 percent of soldiers' families needed aid in 1938, versus 10 percent in peacetime.
overview: This file consists of two detailed intelligence reports compiled in June 1938 by Major Harry I. T. Creswell, the U.S. Military Attaché in Tokyo, and forwarded through the War Department's Military Intelligence Division to the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs under decimal file 894.14 (Philanthropic Organizations). Together, the reports provide an exhaustive survey of Japan's dual public-private relief apparatus established to support mobilized soldiers, wounded veterans, and their dependents following the outbreak of the war in China. Report No. 9415 (June 3, 1938) breaks down the provisions of the revised 1904 Military Relief Law, itemizing statutory scales for cost-of-living allowances, medical and maternity subsidies, occupational transition aid, disability and bereavement pensions, and special civic preferences. Report No. 9452 (June 29, 1938) supplements this with extensive comparative tables analyzing nine major quasi-governmental and private patriotic welfare associations, detailing their specific fields of assistance, supervising government ministries, and leadership rosters comprising Imperial princes, peerage nobles, and high-ranking military officers.

subfiles.about: Detailed intelligence report examining statutory Japanese governmental military relief, disability pensions, and family aid following the outbreak of the war in China.
subfiles.from: Major Harry I. T. Creswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This report examines the statutory structure and recent amendments of Japan's Military Relief Law of 1904 necessitated by large-scale mobilization during the war in China. In contrast to peacetime when only ten percent of mobilized soldiers' families needed public assistance, current wartime conditions required relief for approximately thirty percent. The report details sliding-scale living grants for dependents in urban and rural areas, medical and maternity subsidies, business startup and vocational training aid, bereavement gratuities, and disability pensions for soldiers. It also outlines institutional support such as asylums and vocational institutes for wounded veterans, employment protection for discharged servicemen, and socioeconomic privileges including monopoly licenses for selling tobacco and stamps.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 9415: Philanthropic Organizations - Military Relief (Governmental)
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department (forwarded to Department of State)

subfiles.about: Comprehensive survey and comparative activity matrix of nine major Japanese patriotic and private philanthropic organizations assisting soldiers and their dependents.
subfiles.from: Major Harry I. T. Creswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This report analyzes nine prominent Japanese quasi-governmental and private charitable organizations supplementing official military relief under the supervision of the Home, War, and Navy Ministries. Through detailed comparative tables, it delineates each organization's role in supplying living subsidies, medical and hospitalization assistance, vocational retraining, employment protection, condolence funds, and social guidance for soldiers and bereaved families. A directory provides headquarters addresses, supervising ministries, and officers for all nine bodies, highlighting leadership by Imperial princes, nobility, and senior army and navy officers. Creswell concludes that these popular and well-funded patriotic networks effectively reach into personal spheres untouched by state agencies, significantly bolstering national morale.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 9452: Philanthropic Organizations - Private Relief
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division (G-2), War Department (forwarded to Department of State)
